mortal
(θνατός [mortal] Doric form, not infrequently changed by scribes into the common form) mortal.
Much more frequently used as a substantive.
Thus I corrected for τὰν Διὸς ἁρμονίαν θνατῶν παρεξίασι βουλαί [the harmony of Zeus do the counsels of mortals transgress].
Never do the counsels of mortal men transgress the harmony of Zeus.

to sit

to sit. This verb, which has the meaning of moving quickly, is used for θάσσω [to sit] or Homeric θαάσσω [to sit] by Aeschylus Suppl. 595 ὑπ᾿ ἀρχᾶς δ᾽ οὔτινος θοάζων [sitting under no authority] and Sophocles OR. 2 τίνας ποθ᾽ ἕδρας τάσδε μοι θοάζετε; [what seats are these you are sitting on for me?] which seats do you sit for me, i.e. with what intention have you occupied these seats before my house? where see what I said in the Oxford annotation.

Of ships, as often in Homer, I restored the reading

which are read thus in M, corrupt and interpolated: αἱ δ᾽ ὁμόπτεροι κυανώπιδες | νᾶες μὲν ἄγαγον ποποῖ | νᾶες πανωλέθροισιν ἐμβολαῖς [the dark-eyed ships with like wings brought, alas, ships with all-destroying rammings]. Similarly Arist. Eq. 554 καὶ κυανέμβολοι θοαὶ μισθοφόροι τριήρεις [and dark-beaked swift mercenary triremes].
